solution_overview:
A university tracked pass rates across three exams: Exam A, Exam B, and Exam C. We are given the probabilities of passing individual exams, pairs of exams, and all three exams. One student is selected at random. We will use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for events $A$, $B$, and $C$ representing passing Exams A, B, and C, respectively.

The given probabilities are:
$P(A) = 0.70$
$P(B) = 0.55$
$P(C) = 0.48$

$P(A \cap B) = 0.38$
$P(A \cap C) = 0.32$
$P(B \cap C) = 0.28$

$P(A \cap B \cap C) = 0.20$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The probability that the student passed at least one exam is given by the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three events:

$$P(A \cup B \cup C) = \sum P(X) - \sum P(X \cap Y) + P(A \cap B \cap C)$$

Substituting the given values:

$$P(A \cup B \cup C) = (P(A) + P(B) + P(C)) - (P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap C) + P(B \cap C)) + P(A \cap B \cap C)$$

$$P(A \cup B \cup C) = (0.70 + 0.55 + 0.48) - (0.38 + 0.32 + 0.28) + 0.20$$

$$P(A \cup B \cup C) = 1.73 - 0.98 + 0.20$$

$$P(A \cup B \cup C) = 0.95$$

This is $95\%$, which is above $90\%$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The probability that the student passed exactly one exam can be found by taking the sum of individual probabilities, subtracting two times the sum of pairwise probabilities (since these regions are counted twice in the first sum and once in the second), and adding three times the probability of passing all three exams (since this region was added three times, subtracted six times, and added three times).

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - 2 \cdot (P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap C) + P(B \cap C)) + 3 \cdot P(A \cap B \cap C)$$

Substituting the given values:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = (0.70 + 0.55 + 0.48) - 2 \cdot (0.38 + 0.32 + 0.28) + 3 \cdot 0.20$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 1.73 - 2 \cdot 0.98 + 3 \cdot 0.20$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 1.73 - 1.96 + 0.60$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.37$$

This is $37\%$, which exceeds $35\%$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The probability that the student passed exactly two exams can be found by summing the probabilities of passing each pair, and then subtracting three times the probability of passing all three exams, because the triple intersection region is included in each of the three pairwise probabilities.

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap C) + P(B \cap C) - 3 \cdot P(A \cap B \cap C)$$

Substituting the given values:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.38 + 0.32 + 0.28 - 3 \cdot 0.20$$

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.98 - 0.60$$

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.38$$

This is $38\%$, which is not at least $40\%$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The probability that the student passed none of the three exams is the complement of passing at least one exam.

$$P(\text{none}) = 1 - P(A \cup B \cup C)$$

From statement A, we found $P(A \cup B \cup C) = 0.95$.

$$P(\text{none}) = 1 - 0.95$$

$$P(\text{none}) = 0.05$$

This is $5\%$, which is under $8\%$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The probability that the student passed at least two exams is the sum of the probabilities of passing exactly two exams and passing exactly three exams.

$$P(\text{at least two}) = P(\text{exactly two}) + P(A \cap B \cap C)$$

From statement C, we found $P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.38$. We are given $P(A \cap B \cap C) = 0.20$.

$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.38 + 0.20$$

$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.58$$

This is $58\%$, which exceeds $55\%$, so the statement is True.
